extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature (scientists, researchers, and scholarly readers across physics, chemistry, engineering, ethnography and related fields)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging scientific theories, technical and philosophical books, engineering texts, reference works, and ethnographic studies — as articulated in Nature editorials and book reviews. Emphasises empirical adequacy, audience alignment, accuracy, method, and practical usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for experimental wireless licences (Wireless Telegraphy Act clause 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Where the applicant for a licence proves to the satisfaction of the Postmaster-General that the sole object of obtaining the licence is to enable him to conduct experiments in wireless telegraphy, a licence for that purpose shall be granted, subject to such special terms, conditions and restrictions as the Postmaster-General may think proper, but shall not be subject to any rent or royalty.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licence applicants must demonstrate the sole object is experimental work; licences may have special terms but no rent/royalty; amateurs and trained scientific workers have an equal claim provided they can satisfy the Postmaster-General that the station is experimental (not commercial). The Post Office should avoid making conditions so exacting as to exclude amateurs, who should receive encouragement; overly restrictive departmental rules may provoke evasion of regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and limits on corporate control in broadcasting arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Membership of the proposed broadcasting company will not, of itself, entitle a member to use the patents of other members; the Postmaster-General's attempt to control broadcasting by means of the proposed articles of association is of doubtful wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed articles of association and any provisions that would affect patent rights or control of broadcasting should be made public and not be used to unduly restrict access or competition; avoid opaque contractual provisions that centralize control without scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific theory evaluation — empirical adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific theory must account for the experimental results obtained; older conceptions (e.g., hydrate formation) may be insufficient to explain observed facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theories should be judged by their ability to explain experimental observations. Even theories with some experimental support (e.g., hydrone theory) must be scrutinized for unverifiable assumptions. A theory is not to be discarded lightly — it must be 'killed' by evidence before being abandoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific theory evaluation — usefulness as a working hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The ionic hypothesis … as a working hypothesis gives qualitative and quantitative explanation of a large number of chemical phenomena which can otherwise only be accounted for in a vague and unsatisfactory way.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond pure truth, a valuable hypothesis is one that provides usable qualitative and quantitative explanations and opens new lines of research; efficacy as a research tool and explanatory power are key evaluative criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match between book content and intended audience / prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: Books should be appropriate to the reader’s background: e.g., Planck’s philosophical/theoretical work 'presupposes a knowledge of mathematics' and will appeal to the pure theorist while offering little direct help to the experimenter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and reviewers should assess whether a work’s level and prerequisites (mathematical/philosophical background) align with its stated audience; clarity about prerequisites is important for prospective readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of exposition and instructive examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Textbooks should provide clear descriptions of main phenomena and numerous instructive examples (as praised in Occhialini’s book).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear presentation and worked examples aid learning; reviewers should note pedagogical clarity and the usefulness of examples for students and practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of definitions and technical detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions must be accurate for modern requirements — e.g., the review criticises an insufficiently accurate definition of the 'temperature coefficient of metals.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical terms and definitions should be precise and reflect current standards; where multiple related technical concepts exist (volume resistivity, mass resistivity, constant mass resistance) these distinctions should be made explicit to avoid practical errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: State limitations and domain of applicability of formulae
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximate formulae (e.g., for the self-induction of a coil) should have their limitations stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should indicate the assumptions and limitations of approximate formulae and methods so readers know when they apply and when they fail; reviewers should call out omissions of such caveats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicality and usefulness for practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical engineering works must address applied questions such as what kind of electric machine is required for special work, efficiency, heating under load, insulation strength, and guarantees to demand from manufacturers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A technical/practical book should be judged on how well it helps practitioners make concrete decisions (machine selection, specification, guarantees). Omit overly theoretical material that lacks practical guidance if the book purports to be for practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority, factual accuracy and up-to-dateness in reference works
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference works must exhibit authority and accuracy; the Oil Encyclopedia is criticised for loose or erroneous definitions (e.g., of 'zolian' and 'Cambrian') and incorrect facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encyclopaedic/reference texts should be carefully checked for factual correctness and updated information; sloppy or outdated entries undermine utility and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scope and proportionate coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference works should proportion space to topics by their importance and include terms relevant to the target user; inclusion of biographies and excessive national focus (e.g., undue space to Great Britain) can be misproportioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should balance breadth and depth: avoid extraneous material that crowds out essential technical terms; ensure coverage is proportionate to global importance and usefulness for the intended readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of mere compilation — interpretive and forward-looking analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic/scientific surveys should not be dry compilations of statistics but should use past and present facts to foreshadow future possibilities (praised in Pogue's Economics of Petroleum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works in economics or broad surveys gain value by synthesising data into insightful, predictive narratives rather than becoming unreadable blue-book-like compilations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethnographic method and primary documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethnography should be a well-considered study in method and include documentary evidence: e.g., large numbers of magical formulae and oral texts in the native language with translation are praised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good ethnographic practice includes rigorous fieldwork description, transparent methodological remarks, presentation of primary texts and translations, and ample documentary evidence to support interpretation and enable future researchers to assess claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive insight and psychological explanation in ethnography
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond description, ethnographic works should explain the psychological significance of customs (e.g., Malinowski explains how Kula pervades life and functions similarly to religion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews value ethnographies that interpret social meaning and function of observed practices, connecting description to psychology and social norms rather than mere cataloguing of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation quality: illustrations and accessibility (cost)
rubrics_metrics.description: Books that are well illustrated and of reasonable cost are commended (e.g., Chautard's volume is 'profusely illustrated' and 'inexpensive and necessary').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality illustrations, maps, diagrams and affordable pricing increase a book’s value to its audience; reviewers should note presentation and cost as factors in overall assessment.
